The year is split into four seasons that last 12 days each. Spring - Moderate temperature. Rain and fog are frequent. Small chance of hailstorms. Summer - High temperatures. Chance of heatwaves. Build underground storage to keep your food fresh during the hot summer days. Autumn - Moderate temperature. Rain and fog are frequent. Chance of thunderstorms and hailstorms. Winter - Low temperatures. High chance of snowfall and blizzards. Chance of cold snaps. Vegetation will not grow in low temperatures, so ensure that you sow and harvest as much as you can before winter starts.

Job Priorities - The JOB panel is where you can prioritize each settler's tasks. - By default, settlers will prioritize their jobs from left to right. - Using and , you can change job priorities so that a given settler will choose one job before another. - Jobs set to the same priority level will be prioritized left to right. - If the job box is empty, that means that a settler will never do that job. - Settlers will always do the highest priority job that they can find. - If a specific job is not on anyone's priority list, that job will never get done. - The frame colour of a job box indicates the settler's skill level. Tip - If a settler has a very low skill rating for a specific job, it is better to turn that job off completely for that settler - otherwise, there is a chance they'll do the job and fail. This is important when it comes to things like harvesting. Example: a settler with a low botanical skill level could end up ruining the harvest, yielding no resources. So it's best to let them focus on what they do best!

Welcome To Going Medieval\n- Please bear in mind that the game is under Heavy development. This means that the game will have some bugs and unfinished systems. You can consult the Almanac for help and tutorials.

<style=AlmParagraph>Mood
</style>- Mood represents your settlers' happiness.
- Be sure to check on your settlers’ mood often.
- A low mood can result in settlers rebelling and refusing to follow orders.
- If a settler's mood reaches 0, they will leave your settlement.
- Things like cooked or lavish meals, comfortable beds, and a fair amount of leisure time can help keep your settlers’ spirits high.

<style=AlmParagraph>Manage\n</style>- Use the manage panel to determine which items your settlers will auto-equip, what food and alcohol they are allowed to consume, etc.\n- You can still force settlers to consume or equip something using the right-click action menu.

<style=AlmParagraph>Defence
</style>- Use structures like merlons to your advantage to cover your archers from enemy projectiles.
- Place archers on higher ground so they get a buff in precision, range, and critical hit chance.
- Place traps strategically around your settlement to weaken your enemies.

<style=AlmParagraph>Forbid/Allow
</style>- Settlers will not interact with items that are marked as forbidden.
- Forbidden items will have a forbidden sign over them.
- You can allow forbidden items by using the allow order or by selecting the item and selecting the allow action.

<style=AlmParagraph>Bartering
</style>- Bartering functions by exchanging resources and items with a Merchant.
- You can request resources only if you proffer something in return with the same or similar value.
- The settler making the trade can influence prices, and can also negotiate to get more than they offered.

- Giving the merchant more value than is received will be considered a gift, and will influence alignment favourably towards the Merchant's faction.
- The value of resources is determined by merchant type, faction, alignment, and even time of year.

Region\n- You can see what factions and faction settlements are in your region.\n- Form a caravan and send your settlers to trade with other settlements by selecting a settlement and clicking the send caravan button.

<style=AlmParagraph>Alignment\n</style>- Alignment determines whether a faction is friendly, neutral or hostile towards your settlement.\n- Hostile factions will initiate raids on your settlement, while friendly and neutral factions will send Merchants your way from time to time.
Initiate Bartering\n- To initiate bartering with a merchant, select a settler and on the merchant, then select the Barter with option.

<style=AlmParagraph>Relocate Structures
</style>- Smaller structures like furniture, workstations and decorations can be easily relocated: Select an already-constructed structure and click on the relocate button. Then select a new location.

- Structures that are removed will turn into a resource pile and can be stored on stockpiles, and even traded with Merchants.

<style=AlmParagraph>Farming
</style>- Sow crop fields to ensure a steady supply of food for the upcoming winter. 
- Choose a crop from the zone panel [<style=Shortcut>F7</style>], then drag it to the required size.
- You need appropriate supplies of seeds and saplings in order to sow.
- New varieties of crop fields will be unlocked as you acquire new seed types, either by foraging, or from merchants. 
- Remember that plants need sunlight. Sow crops in the open, away from trees or structures that will create shade. Days are shorter in winter and early spring, so try to avoid sowing plants during this time.

Animals Wild Animals - Settlers can hunt and butcher wild animals for meat and leather. - Some animals like wolves and boars have a chance to retaliate when hunted. - To hunt an animal, a settler needs to be equipped with a ranged weapon. Domestic Animals - Some wild animals can be tamed. - Some animals may attack a settler who is trying to tame them, so beware. -Taming can be a long process and can't be done continually. Settlers can try to tame an animal once every 24h. - Tamed animals will live alongside settlers. Some animals can be kept in animal pens. To create a pen, place a pen marker in a fenced off or enclosed area. Pets - Some domestic animals can be trained to become pets. - Pets can be assigned to settlers so that they will follow them around and even help out around the settlement.

- All items like weapons, armour and apparel have a quality level. - Quality levels are: flimsy, sturdy, good, fine, superior and flawless. - Higher quality levels mean the item is more durable, and has better attributes, such as damage or range. Some items may have different modifiers depending on their quality. - Your settlers have a higher chance of producing better quality items if their skill in that field is higher. - When highly-skilled settlers are in a good mood, their chances of producing a flawless item will also increase slightly.

<style=AlmParagraph>Outside & Inside Temperature
</style>- Outdoor temperature is shown in the top right corner of the screen next to the time.
- This temperature is the global outdoor temperature that is further modified by sunlight, shade, proximity to heat sources, etc. 
- Outdoor temperature depends on the season, time of day and active weather events such as cold snaps or heatwaves.
- You can inspect temperature using the temperature overlay on the upper left panel <sprite="temp_overlay_text_icon" index=t>. 
- To view indoor temperature, mouse over a room. Its temperature will be displayed replacing the outdoor temperature reading, in the top right corner. Alternatively, select the room to see this information.
- Indoor temperature depends on the outdoor temperature, and the room's insulation, as well as elements that have thermal output inside the room, like torches or a campfire.
<style=AlmParagraph>
Keeping cold
</style>If you want to have a colder room during the summertime, you can:
- build a room underground. 
- use material that has high insulation, such as clay.
- keep windows open and extinguish all heat sources inside that room.
- Note that windows that let sunlight in can also heat up the room
- Store ice blocks to further cool the area around them. 
<style=AlmParagraph>
Keeping warm
</style>If you want to have warm rooms during the wintertime, you can:
- place heat sources inside the rooms.
- close all windows to keep the warmth inside.

<style=AlmParagraph><sprite="damage_icon" index=t>Damage 
</style>- Damage is calculated from several factors: attackers' attributes; weapon base damage; weapon armour penetration; and the opponents’ armour rating and armour durability.
- If the attacker hits an opponent without armour, then the entire damage will be inflicted and the opponents’ HP will be lowered by that amount.
- If the attacker hits an opponent who is wearing armour, then the damage is affected by the weapon's armour penetration attribute and the opponents’ armour rating and armour hitpoint percentage.

- The formula for dealing damage is:

<style=Desc>(weapon base damage * armour penetration) - ((weapon base damage * armour penetration) * (armour hit points percentage at that moment * armour rating))</style>
<style=AlmParagraph>
<sprite="critical_strike" index=t> Critical Damage
</style>- Every attack has a 15% chance to deal critical damage by striking the opponent in the head.
All critical damage is multiplied by 2x.
- When critical damage is inflicted, the damage takes into consideration headgear instead of body armour.
<style=AlmParagraph>
<sprite="range_icon" index=t> Range
</style>- The number of grid spaces the weapon can reach. 
<style=AlmParagraph>
<sprite="precision_icon" index=t> Precision
</style>- The weapon's chance to hit the target.
- This is not the weapon's final chance to hit its target.
- The chance to hit is affected by things like: the attackers’ attributes, precision falloff with distance, weather and terrain elevation.
<style=AlmParagraph>
Precision falloff with distance
</style>- This is the  percentage the chance to hit falls as the target gets further away.
<style=AlmParagraph>
Armour penetration
</style>- This is the percentage of damage that will pass through armour. Piercing weapons like spears, arrows and bolts have a high armour penetration percentage.
<style=AlmParagraph>
Armour damage
</style>- This is the percentage of base damage that will be inflicted to the armour or shield (or headgear if critical strike) Weapons like hammers and maces as well as axes have a high armour damage percentage, so they are ideal for armoured opponents or breaking down their shields
<style=AlmParagraph>
Building damage
</style>- The percentage of base damage that will be inflicted on buildings, workbenches and furniture. Blunt weapons and axes have a high building damage percentage. They are ideal for taking down doors.

<style=AlmParagraph><sprite="body_armor_icon" index=t> Armour rating
</style>- Armour rating further reduces the incoming damage after the armour penetration weapon attribute is taken into account. The higher the armour rating the better. 
- Armour rating reduces as the armour piece loses its HP.
<style=AlmParagraph>
<sprite="cover_icon" index=t> Cover amount
</style>- A shield's cover amount is the amount of incoming attacks the shield will absorb. Damage is fully absorbed by the shield but the shield takes the damage (multiplied by the weapon's armour damage).
- The final percentage of incoming blows absorbed is the shield cover amount + the opponent's evade chance attribute.

<style=AlmParagraph><sprite="temperature_min_icon" index=t> Minimum comfortable temperature
</style>- Clothing can adjust the wearer's minimum comfortable temperature so that they are less affected by the cold. In the case of winter clothing, the wearer can withstand lower temperatures without negative effects. E.g.: A settler's minimum comfortable temperature is 3°C but winter clothing adds -20°C. The settler's effective minimum comfortable temperature is now -17°C.
<style=AlmParagraph>
<sprite="temperature_max_icon" index=t> Maximum comfortable temperature
</style>- Clothing can also adjust the wearer's maximum comfortable temperature. In the case of summer clothing, this means that they withstand higher temperatures without negative effects.

Certain resources and items can decompose or rot Reasons for decomposition and rotting: - Being outdoors - Leaving your resources to get affected by the rain or snow will make them decompose faster. Place a roof over your stockpile to stop this from happening. - Temperature - Resources like food will decompose faster during the summer - Ground-type - Don’t leave your resources on the ground. Build floors underneath your stockpile zones to slow down decomposition.

Some resources like curdling milk can ferment if the temperature is right. Resources that ferment will turn into new resources after the fermentation process is finished. Example: Curdling milk will turn into cheese.

- Each structure has a stability value. - This determines whether you can attach other structures to it. - When set on the ground, a structure has a stability value of 4. Each structure attached to it will have -1 stability the further away it is placed. - You cannot position a structure with a stability value of 0. - The vertical stability value remains unchanged. - To view the stability values around your current cursor position, turn the stability visualizer on. Beams - Place beams between two walls or terrain voxels. If one of these gets destroyed, this will also destroy the beam and everything resting on it. - A beam has a maximum range of 10 grid spaces. - The beam will inherit the lower stability value of the two walls/voxels it ties together. - Walls, windows, doors, roofs, merlons, and floors are the only things that you can place on beams.

- Use the SCHEDULE panel to choose when settlers do each type of activity. - Work time is when settlers will do the jobs assigned in the JOBS panel. - Leisure is for eating, playing, and religious activities. TIP: Some settlers are more productive at different times than others - check their perks!

- To control your settlers directly, you need to draft them.
- Draft settlers by selecting them, then clicking the draft action.
- You can also select settlers from the settler panel on the left.

<style=Desc>TIP: You can select multiple settlers by dragging over them or using [<style=Shortcut>Shift</style>] + <sprite="ctrl_left_click" index=t>. Then you can draft them all at once.</style>

- Your settlers need somewhere to store resources.
- You can choose where they store things by setting up a Stockpile Zone.
- Select the Zone panel in the lower left of the screen, or press [<style=Shortcut><input:Zone></style>].
- Choose the Default Stockpile, then select an area for the stockpile.

<style=Desc>TIP: Place stockpiles on floors and under roofs to slow down resources' decay.
TIP: Click on a placed stockpile to change what settlers will and won't store inside it.</style>

- Mood represents your settlers' happiness.
- Check on your settlers' mood often, by selecting them and then the Mood category.
- A low mood can result in settlers rebelling and refusing to follow orders.
- If a settler's mood reaches 0, they will leave your settlement.
- Things like cooked or lavish meals, comfortable beds, and leisure time can help keep your settlers' spirits high.

- Use the Manage panel to set which items your settlers can auto-equip and consume.

<style=Desc>TIP: You can override these settings by selecting a settler and forcing them to equip or consume something by right-clicking on the item and selecting an action</style>

- Create spots for archers on high ground to buff their precision, range, and crit chance.\n- Use structures like merlons to cover your archers from enemy projectiles.\n- Place traps strategically around your settlement to weaken your enemies.

- Items are either forbidden or allowed. Settlers will not interact with forbidden items.
- Forbidden items will have a sign over them: a hand with a cross.
- You can allow items using the order in the bottom right of the screen.
- Forbid items by selecting them and then clicking the forbid action.

<style=Desc>TIP: By default, most loose items on a new map are forbidden.
TIP: You may wish to forbid settlers from retrieving items like dead bodies or rotten food.</style>

- You can exchange resources and items with merchants.
- The items you offer should have the same or a similar value to those you ask for.
- You can gift items to the merchant by offering more value than you receive.
- This will favourably influence the merchant's faction towards you.
- Resources' value depends on merchant type, faction, alignment, and even time of year.

- You can see what factions and settlements are in your region via the Region map.
-Here you will be able to see the neighboring factions, occasional bandit camps, and other points of interest. 

-Keep in mind that what you do in your settlement will be noticed by others in your region. Various types of <LinkAlmanac="Gameplaytipsrenown">renown</link> can be gained and will be recognised by others.

- The way you build your settlement and the things you do will change your renown.
-When renown of any type reaches 100% you will be given the choice to pursue a Grand Objective that will lead your settlement into the endgame. 

- Renown may be influenced by your settlers' roles, events you hold, and the outcomes of battles.

- Alignment determines whether a faction is friendly, neutral or hostile towards your settlement.\n- Hostile factions will initiate raids on your settlement, while friendly and neutral factions will send Merchants your way from time to time.

- To barter with a merchant, select a settler and on the merchant, then select the Barter With option. TIP: The settler making the trade can influence prices and negotiate, so try to send someone with high speechcraft.

- Furniture, workstations, and other small constructions can be easily relocated
- Select an item of furniture and click the relocate button, then select a new location.
- You can also remove structures.
- Removed structures turn into resource piles and can be stored or traded.

- Crop fields ensure a steady supply of food, even in winter.
- Choose a crop from the zone panel [<style=Shortcut><input:Zone></style>], then drag it to the required size.
- You must have stockpiled seeds or saplings in order to sow crops.
- New varieties of crop will unlock as you forage or buy new seed types.

<style=Desc>TIP: Plants need sunlight - sow seeds away from trees or structures that create shade.</style>

- Settlers can hunt and butcher wild animals for meat and leather.\n- Some animals like wolves and boars have a chance to retaliate when hunted.\n- To hunt an animal, a settler must be equipped with a ranged weapon.
- Some wild animals can be tamed.\n- Beware: some animals may attack a settler who is trying to tame them.\n- Taming can be a long process and cannot be done continually.

- Domestic animals live alongside settlers.
- Some animals may be kept in animal pens. 
- To create a pen, place a <LinkAlmanac="Penmarker">pen marker</link> in a fenced-off or enclosed area.
- Add a <LinkAlmanac="Trough">trough</link> to your pen so that settlers will automatically bring food to the penned animals.
- Settlers can use their animal handling skill to gain food from some animals.
- Some domestic animals can also be slaughtered for meat.
- Some domestic animals can be trained to become pets.\n- Pets can be assigned to settlers so that they will follow them around and even help out around the settlement.
- Some structures, like walls, fences and roofs, have visual variations that can be selected to customise their appearance. These variations are purely aesthetic and don't influence gameplay.

- Certain events can be triggered, like a <LinkAlmanac="Playertriggeredeventfeast">Feast</link> or a <LinkAlmanac="Playertriggeredeventsermon">Sermon</link>. 
- To launch these events, construct the corresponding room type, and select the structure within it which is the origin of the event. 
- Each event type has conditions, and will have varying levels of quality, depending on which conditions are met. 
- Different quality outcomes will result in different mood and other buffs or debuff to the event's participants. 
- Some events benefit from having a settler with a <LinkAlmanac="Roletypes">role</link> present.

The Church of the Third Coming
The Philosophers of the Natural Order
No affiliation with any faction. Harming a nonpartisan will not trigger any friendliness penalties. But it may have other repercussions.

An often brutal, neochristian theocracy, disciples preach that the plague marked the beginning of Armageddon, in a world ruled by Satan and his demons. They keenly await the return of Christ and have joined the final battle to purify the world of sin and sinners, by any means necessary. Militant and aggressive, they have barely any understanding for those who lack their faith.

A band of Christian mystics proselytising the obscure, visionary dreams of Anchoress Menwreda of Wigmore, who was walled into a cell for life at just 15 years of age. Her complex, mystic revelations calcified into rigid doctrine during the plague years. Adherents frequently burn people alive, accusing them of being in league with the Devil, the cause of the scourge.

Plantagenet Royalists, the Faithful champion Edmund II as the lawful heir to the throne. Their goal is to reunite England, recreating the feudal structure that was in place before the pestilence, with Edmund’s favourite, Sir Hugh Gaveston, leading the charge.

A rough collective of factions led by individual barons, united by their unswerving loyalty to the former queen, Isabella of France. Backed by the powerful house of Aquitaine and using not just military might but also necromancy, this group aims to reinstate the nobility and ensure its longevity.

These scholars argue that Nature, and not God, wrought the plague. Zealously pursuing knowledge, they pore over tomes of Byzantine scripture and debate Ockham's law of parsimony. They dream of a new world order based on study, not superstition, girding themselves with learning to ward of future pestilence.

Intellectuals led by the flamboyant alchemist, Gaius Ortolanus, the Society of Fellows aims to distil understanding of the plague to its quintessence, and so, obtain mastery over it. Rigorous, serious, and often cantankerous, they suppress ignorance and religious claptrap wherever they find it.

This newly-founded anti-kingdom is led by firebrand peasant, Jan Purvey. He lays the blame for the plague squarely on the English Crown, and its warfare against France. Without this folly, Britain would have kept this pestilence at its borders with the continent, namely, the English Channel. The York movement calls for permanent abolition of the monarchy, and equal rights for all.

Inspired by the mystic Marguerite Porete, who was burnt at the stake for heresy, followers strive towards the annihilation of the soul. Beyond this, some are nihilists, many think they are God, and most despise hierarchies. The only thing they agree upon is their right to disagree. Their motto is: 'where there is order, let me bring chaos.'

Arthur Pendragon and his stately court epitomise Britain’s golden era. So says the Circle of Avalon, which strives for a renaissance of chivalry and knightly virtue. Once upon a time, Merlin's second sight revealed fearsome dragons battling beneath Vortigern’s castle. Today, the Circle calls on his druid successors to restore the old ways, summoning a ray of light in a these darkening days.

The ancient oral tradition of gathering poetry and lore is strong, and of all the corners of Britain, this practice is most exalted in the valleys of Wales. Beirdd ⁠— bards ⁠— become initiates by sleeping on Cadair Idris, learn of shapeshifting from Taliesin, and celebrate Gwledd Brân, the Feast of the Crow. Bards become adept at casting a spell over listeners, finally becoming tutors and completing the cycle.

A group of marauders, thieves and slavers, the Progeny flourish due to drinking the blood of plague survivors. Their practices have evolved to include ritual torture, savagery and dismemberment. They hunt humans as they would any wild animal, taking pleasure in the thrill of the chase. Captives are livestock: bred, worked to death and eaten. These cannibals are now so feared, that it is hard to discern where the stories end, and the horror begins.

Among the many prohibitions in the Bible, none appears against eating human flesh. Upon this flimsy scaffold, the Ravagers — driven first by starvation, and later by developing culinary practices — have built their rationale for a cannibalistic lifestyle. Their recipe books feature detailed instructions to turn almost all body parts into haute cuisine: roasts, sausages, charcuterie…some of which they sell to hungry villagers, unaware of what — or whom — they are consuming.

Moving silently among ancient oaks and living on wild game, nettles and roots, life in the forest depths comes naturally to many a felon. What could be more companionable than gathering around the fire, sharing tales of the Hyrne and his Wild Hunt, and planning the next raid?

Rugged and weathered, the mountain clans shelter in natural caves and bathe under icy waterfalls. Clad in wolfskins and hunting in packs, they slink down from their mountain strongholds to strike: silent, ferocious, hungry.

Britain’s mighty rivers carry waterfolk, who in turn ferry travelers, goods and news. Since the sickness, they have become indigent and feral, embracing piracy and pillage. The wherrymen make offerings to the nymph queen, Coventina, at the riverside, hopeful that she will bless their predatory riverine incursions.

When the plague took hold, authority crumbled and hunger stalked the land. Mercenaries, robber barons and displaced peasants roamed unchecked, preying on the weak. These looters take whatever they can carry, and will maim and kill with impunity.

Some say that they are revenant plague victims. Their faces are always covered. And, since their corpses catch alight and turn to ash, disturbing uncertainty lingers as to who, or what, they are. Their presence is invoked if milk sours, or a child goes missing in the night. Beasts are found cruelly dispatched, but not eaten. Crops are burned, items smashed. They exist only to manifest terror, and their name, seldom spoken, is the Scourge.

EDEN NOVA
Eden Nova is a newly-built settlement. It grew up around the abbey founded by St Augustine in Canterbury, where the Roman monk rekindled Christianity among the pagan Saxons, eventually spreading it across the land. A birthplace of new ideas, Eden Nova harbours a fundamentalist Christian sect, intent on converting a new generation of sinners.

HEREFORD
Hereford Tower is a great structure encasing the former cell, and now tomb, of the visionary Anchoress Menwreda at Wigmore Abbey. It has become a site of pilgrimage and a power base for the Ancrene Disciples.

NEW EXETER
New Exeter was founded outside the original city walls, after Exeter’s Bishop fled during the plague. Work on the cathedral had ground to a halt, and 1900 died, leaving Devon’s former first city desolate.

LANCASTER
A fortification crouched on a bend of the River Lune, Lancaster boasts a fine castle, built to repel the Scots. Members of the Plantagenet dynasty ruling over this earldom perished in the great sickness. It has a reputation for notable imprisonments, and executions.

OXFORD
Built to ford the river Thames and surrounded by marshes, Oxford was latterly a meeting place of royalty, but since the plague, has fallen from grace. All sects of scholars and religious orders dwell here, often quarrelling among themselves while reaching for the truth.

CAMBRIDGE
In the eastern fenlands lies Cambridge, once a Roman trading post, now a place of learning, religion, and frequent riots. Without a king or archbishop to back their cause, the scholars are often besieged by resentful and untrusting townsfolk.

YORK
Once home to Roman armies and Viking heroes, York is the great capital of the North. Beneath its cobbled streets run ancient Roman sewers and other hidden passageways. From this obscure warren, the Kingdom of York sends forth its footsoldiers and spies.

ROSSLYN
The dungeons beneath Rosslyn Castle are said to hide a clandestine library of dangerous and esoteric texts, closely guarded by Heretics. The nobles who lived here having perished, a dense, almost impenetrable forest has grown up around it. Frightening stories are spread to keep it undisturbed.

GLASTONBURY
According to legend, it was here at the Isle of Glass that Excalibur was forged and here, grievously wounded, that Arthur sought respite after the Battle of Camlann. It is told that Morgan le Fay and her eight sisters practiced the healing arts here, and that there is a hidden cave through which you can pass to the fairy realm of Annwn. The Circle of Avalon has raised a new Mithraeum, atop the tor.

YNIS MÔN
The Beirdd Cymraeg inhabit the island of Ynys Môn, around the great burial chamber Bryn Celli Ddu. The island has long been a seat of bardic and druidic learning. There the Roman chronicler Tacitus met 'Furies, in robes of deathly black and with dishevelled hair,' and 'a circle of Druids, lifting their hands to heaven.'

ISLE OF MANN
An island formed when an Irish giant threw a clod of earth at a rival in Scotland. It missed, and fell into the Irish sea, becoming the Isle of Mann. It lies under the misty cloak of the sea god, Manannán, who gave immortality to the gods through his swine, which returned to life when killed; those who ate of the swine never died.

NOVA FORESTA
Nova Foresta was proclaimed a Royal Forest by William the Conqueror. As a result, it is well stocked with game, and is ideal for hunting. Local legends tell of the Ettin, a race of ferocious giants. These tales have been interwoven with recent cannibal sightings. So this regal landscape, rich with fauna, is usually avoided.
